newsitem.title: MEXICO: Two dead, 5000 evacuated as Mexico fire rages.
newsitem.headline: Two dead, 5000 evacuated as Mexico fire rages.

text.p: Two people died of their burns on Tuesday and more than 5,000 people were evacuated as firefighters battled an inferno raging for more than a day in three huge fuel tanks that exploded just outside Mexico City.

At least 13 other people were injured, several critically, in Monday afternoon's disaster. Towering columns of flame continued to light up Mexico City's skyline late on Tuesday as thick black smoke billowed three miles (five km) into the air.
State oil monopoly Pemex, which owns the depot where the blast took place, said fireman Jose Luis Romero, 46, and Pemex worker Jose Antonio Ibarra, 34, had died of their burns.

The fire flared up again on Tuesday afternoon and night, leading to radio reports that a fourth tank had exploded. But a Pemex official at the scene said a sudden bolt of flame was caused by a collapsing panel on an already burning tank.

Neither Pemex nor the San Juan Ixhautepec district -- known as San Juanico -- are strangers to such disasters. Monday's blast occurred in the same district where a liquefied petroleum gas explosion 12 years ago burned at least 511 people to death and engulfed homes in flames.

Monday's disaster struck when Pemex workers were repairing a valve in a tank containing 80,000 barrels of fuel at a storage facility, but the exact cause was not known, Pemex chairman Adrian Lajous said early on Tuesday.
Later in the day, Lajous acknowledged "failures" in security and training at the oil giant and said at a news conference that Pemex needed to strengthen both.

Pemex has had three disasters at its facilities in the past two years and in 1992 more than 200 people died when fuel from a Pemex depot leaked into the sewer system in Mexico's second city of Guadalajara and exploded.
"Pemex should designate more resources to ensure the security of its installations...and should consider a profound modification of its industrial practices," Lajous said.
Opposition politicians called for Lajous to resign and for Pemex's management to be completely overhauled.
"It seems ... maintenance and investment in modernizing equipment just does not happen," said Jalisco state Gov. Alberto Cardenas of the conservative National Action Party (PAN).
"It would seem state firms are black boxes where no one has the right to find out what is being invested in what areas ... and today we are paying the consequences."
The Attorney General's Office said it was setting up a special team of experts to investigate the explosion.
Firefighters trained hoses on flames and other nearby
Although Pemex had originally said the blaze would be put out by Tuesday, Pemex workers later said it would take until Wednesday for the more than 105,000 barrels stored in the tanks to burn off.
Residents of this impoverished neighborhood said disasters like Monday's would be repeated unless officials took seriously security concerns at dozens of factories in the area.

"People don't want to live here anymore; it's not safe," said a 64-year-old San Juanico resident who declined to give his name. "Look at all the tanks of gasoline and houses all around. This is a danger zone."
